q: We will notice that every piece is a magnet with a N-pole and ____.
e: We will notice that every piece is a magnet with a N-pole and S-pole. Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole, and like poles push apart.

q: Therefore, it would be reasonable to imagine that if we keep on cutting each piece of the magnet into even smaller pieces, they would still be ____.
e: Therefore, it would be reasonable to imagine that if we keep on cutting each piece of the magnet into even smaller pieces, they would still be magnetised. Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole, and like poles push apart.

q: In other words, we can suppose that the original magnet is made up of lots of magnets all lined up with their N-poles pointing in ____ direction.
e: In other words, we can suppose that the original magnet is made up of lots of magnets all lined up with their N-poles pointing in same direction. Same here means lined up together, which is how a bar becomes magnetised. Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole, and like poles push apart.

q: In other words, we can suppose that the original magnet is made up of lots of magnets all lined up with their N-poles pointing in same ____.
e: In other words, we can suppose that the original magnet is made up of lots of magnets all lined up with their N-poles pointing in same direction. Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole, and like poles push apart.

q: This explains why the poles of the magnet are around the ends as shown in Figure 10.4 which illustrates a magnetised bar composed of ____ magnets.
e: This explains why the poles of the magnet are around the ends as shown in Figure 10.4 which illustrates a magnetised bar composed of tiny magnets. Tiny here means the domain-sized magnets inside a bar. Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole, and like poles push apart.

q: This explains why the poles of the magnet are around the ends as shown in Figure 10.4 which illustrates a magnetised bar composed of tiny ____.
e: This explains why the poles of the magnet are around the ends as shown in Figure 10.4 which illustrates a magnetised bar composed of tiny magnets. Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole, and like poles push apart.

q: In the case of unmagnetised bar, we can imagine the 'tiny' magnets pointing in ____ direction as shown in Figure 10.5.
e: In the case of unmagnetised bar, we can imagine the 'tiny' magnets pointing in random direction as shown in Figure 10.5. Random here means pointing every which way, so the tiny magnets cancel. Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole, and like poles push apart.

q: The resulting magnetic effect of all the tiny magnets is then cancelled out and thus the bar is said to be ____.
e: The resulting magnetic effect of all the tiny magnets is then cancelled out and thus the bar is said to be unmagnetised. Unmagnetised here means having tiny magnets jumbled so their effects cancel. Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole, and like poles push apart.

q: Both the magnetised materials (inclusive of magnets) and unmagnetised materials are made up of ____ magnets.
e: Both the magnetised materials (inclusive of magnets) and unmagnetised materials are made up of tiny magnets. Tiny here means the domain-sized magnets inside a bar. Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole, and like poles push apart.

q: When we take a thin piece of magnetised steel bar and cut it into three smaller ____.
e: When we take a thin piece of magnetised steel bar and cut it into three smaller pieces. Pieces here means each fragment is still a full magnet with two poles.
